# Judges Chapter 20 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), c. 1008 CE | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/JDG_page_289.jpg, JDG_page_290.jpg, JDG_page_291.jpg

1. Then all the people of Israel came out, from Dan to Beersheba, including the land of Gilead, and the congregation assembled as one man to the LORD at Mizpah.

2. The chiefs of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God — 400,000 foot soldiers who drew the sword.

3. (Now the people of Benjamin heard that the people of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.) And the people of Israel said, "Tell us, how did this evil come about?"

4. And the Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered and said, "I came to Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night.

5. "And the leaders of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house against me by night. They intended to kill me, and they violated my concubine, and she died.

6. "So I took hold of my concubine and cut her in pieces and sent her throughout all the territory of the inheritance of Israel, for they have committed lewdness and outrage in Israel.

7. "Behold, all you people of Israel, give here your counsel and advice."

8. And all the people arose as one man, saying, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will return to his house.

9. "But now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot,

10. "and we will take ten men of a hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred of a thousand, and a thousand of ten thousand, to bring provisions for the people, that when they come to Gibeah of Benjamin they may repay them for all the outrage that they have committed in Israel."

11. So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one man.

12. And the tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What is this evil that has taken place among you?

13. "Now therefore hand over the men, the worthless fellows in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the people of Israel.

14. Then the people of Benjamin came together out of the cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the people of Israel.

15. And the people of Benjamin mustered out of their cities on that day 26,000 men who drew the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who mustered 700 chosen men.

16. Among all these people there were 700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.

17. And the men of Israel, apart from Benjamin, mustered 400,000 men who drew the sword; all these were men of war.

18. The people of Israel arose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God, "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Judah shall go up first."

19. Then the people of Israel rose in the morning and encamped against Gibeah.

20. And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up the battle line against them at Gibeah.

21. The people of Benjamin came out of Gibeah and destroyed on that day 22,000 men of Israel.

22. But the people, the men of Israel, took courage, and again formed the battle line in the same place where they had formed it on the first day.

23. And the people of Israel went up and wept before the LORD until the evening. And they inquired of the LORD, "Shall we again draw near for battle against the people of Benjamin, our brother?" And the LORD said, "Go up against him."

24. So the people of Israel came near against the people of Benjamin the second day.

25. And Benjamin went against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed 18,000 men of the people of Israel. All these were men who drew the sword.

26. Then all the people of Israel, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before the LORD and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.

27. And the people of Israel inquired of the LORD (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,

28. and Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, ministered before it in those days), saying, "Shall we go out once more to battle against the people of Benjamin, our brother, or shall we cease?" And the LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand."

29. So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah.

30. And the people of Israel went up against the people of Benjamin on the third day and set themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times.

31. And the people of Benjamin went out against the people and were drawn away from the city. And as at other times they began to strike and kill some of the people in the highways, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, and in the open country, about thirty men of Israel.

32. And the people of Benjamin said, "They are routed before us, as at the first." But the people of Israel said, "Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways."

33. And all the men of Israel rose up out of their place and formed up at Baal-tamar, and the men of Israel who were in ambush rushed out of their place, from the vicinity of Geba.

34. And there came against Gibeah 10,000 chosen men out of all Israel, and the battle was fierce. But the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them.

35. And the LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and the people of Israel destroyed 25,100 men of Benjamin that day. All these were men who drew the sword.

36. So the people of Benjamin saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel gave ground to Benjamin, because they trusted the ambush that they had set against Gibeah.

37. Then the men in ambush hurried and rushed against Gibeah; the men in ambush spread out and struck the whole city with the edge of the sword.

38. Now the appointed signal between the men of Israel and the men in ambush was that when they made a great cloud of smoke rise up out of the city,

39. the men of Israel should turn in battle. Now Benjamin had begun to strike and kill about thirty men of Israel. They said, "Surely they are defeated before us, as in the first battle."

40. But when the signal began to rise out of the city in a column of smoke, the Benjaminites looked behind them, and behold, the whole of the city went up in smoke to heaven.

41. Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster had come upon them.

42. Therefore they turned their backs before the men of Israel in the direction of the wilderness, but the battle overtook them. And those who came out of the cities were destroying them in their midst.

43. They surrounded the Benjaminites, chased them, and trod them down from their resting place as far as opposite Gibeah on the east.

44. Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them men of valor.

45. And they turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. Five thousand men were cut down on the highways. And they were pursued hard to Gidom, and 2,000 men of them were struck down.

46. So all who fell that day of Benjamin were 25,000 men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor.

47. But 600 men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon and remained at the rock of Rimmon for four months.

48. And the men of Israel turned back against the people of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword — the city, men and beasts and all that was found. And all the towns that they found they set on fire.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 20 is the book's narrative nadir — Israel's civil war against Benjamin. The chapter mirrors Israel's conquest narratives but with the enemy replaced by a brother tribe. The literary structure — three battles with escalating desperation, culminating in an ambush strategy identical to the conquest of Ai (Joshua 8) — makes the theological point unmistakable: Israel has become its own worst enemy.

The three inquiries at Bethel (vv.18, 23, 28) chart Israel's spiritual progression: first a confident tactical question ("Who goes first?"), then a shaken question after loss ("Shall we go again?"), finally a broken question after devastating loss ("Shall we go again, or shall we cease?"). Only at the third inquiry, accompanied by fasting and offerings, does God promise victory. The pattern suggests that even righteous anger must be purified by suffering and dependence.

The Phinehas genealogy (v.28) anchors the narrative to early Israel — within two generations of Aaron — contradicting the late-Judges editorial frame. This tension is deliberate: the narrator places the story last for thematic reasons, not chronological ones.

---
## ⚠️ Disagreement Log

### v.5 — "they violated my concubine" vs. "they raped my concubine"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "my concubine they humbled" | innah — standard OT verb for sexual violence |
| LOGOS | "they violated my concubine" | Formal, preserves the legal register |
| PNEUMA | "They raped my concubine" | Modern, unambiguous |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew innah (עָנָּה) is a legal term used throughout the Torah for sexual violence (cf. Deut 22:24, 29; 2 Sam 13:12, 14 — Tamar). It carries juridical weight that English "rape" conveys in modern usage but "violated" preserves in a literary register that matches the Levite's testimony before the assembly. PNEUMA's "raped" is not wrong — it is exactly what happened — but the formal legal context favors the formal term.

**Status:** Moderate. Register choice in a legal assembly context.

---

### v.13 — "worthless fellows" vs. "sons of Belial" vs. "wicked men"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "sons of B'liyya'al" | Transliteration of Hebrew |
| LOGOS | "worthless fellows" | Standard interpretive rendering |
| PNEUMA | "worthless men" | Same sense, slightly different |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. B'nei b'liyya'al is a compound phrase meaning "sons of worthlessness/destruction" — used for the men of Gibeah (19:22), the sons of Eli (1 Sam 2:12), and Nabal (1 Sam 25:17). "Worthless fellows" preserves the contempt without transliterating. EMET's transliteration is opaque; PNEUMA's "worthless men" is functionally identical to LOGOS.

**Status:** Minor. Standard religious vocabulary.

---

### v.18 — "Who shall go up first?" — Echo of 1:1

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Who shall go up first for us to battle against the sons of Binyamin?" | Literal, preserves "sons of" |
| LOGOS | "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" | Formal, same structure as 1:1 |
| PNEUMA | "Which tribe should lead the attack against Benjamin?" | Dynamic, loses the verbal echo |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The phrase mi ya'aleh lanu bat'chilah ("who shall go up for us first?") is identical to 1:1. This is one of the most important literary inclusions in the book — the same question opens the conquest and opens the civil war. PNEUMA's "Which tribe should lead the attack?" loses the verbal parallel entirely. The echo must be preserved.

**Status:** Major. Literary inclusion — the book's structural bookend.

---

### v.34 — "the evil was touching them" vs. "disaster was close upon them" vs. "disaster was about to strike"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "the evil was touching them" | noge'a — literally "touching" |
| LOGOS | "disaster was close upon them" | Interprets naga' as proximity |
| PNEUMA | "disaster was about to strike" | Dynamic, temporal |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew noge'a (נֹגַ֥עַת) from naga' literally means "touching" — the evil/disaster was already in contact with them, they just didn't know it. "Close upon them" captures the imminence better than PNEUMA's "about to strike" (which implies it hasn't yet arrived). EMET's "touching" is technically accurate but sounds odd in English.

**Status:** Minor. Lexical nuance.

---

### v.48 — cherem language: "men and beasts" vs. "everyone — people, animals, everything"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "from the city, men to beast to all that was found" | Preserves m'tom ad-b'hemah |
| LOGOS | "the city, men and beasts and all that was found" | Formal, preserves structure |
| PNEUMA | "putting everyone to the sword — people, animals, everything they found" | Dynamic, adds "putting to sword" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The key phrase is m'ir m'tom ad-b'hemah — "from the city, from men to beast" — which echoes the cherem (holy-war destruction) formula applied to Canaanite cities. The precise wording matters: Israel applies to its own brother tribe the same destruction it was commanded to apply to Canaan. PNEUMA's expansion, while clear, adds "putting to the sword" which dilutes the formula's echo of Deuteronomy 13:15 and Joshua 6:21.

**Status:** Moderate. Cherem vocabulary — connects civil war to holy war.

---

## Summary of Disagreement Patterns

| Pattern | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Literary echo / inclusion | 1 | "Who shall go up first?" (v.18 / 1:1) — book's structural bookend |
| Register in formal context | 1 | innah rendering in assembly testimony (v.5) |
| Cherem vocabulary | 1 | Holy-war language applied to brother tribe (v.48) |
| Standard vocabulary | 1 | B'nei b'liyya'al rendering (v.13) |
| Lexical nuance | 1 | naga' — "touching" vs. "close upon" (v.34) |

**Overall pattern:** The critical disagreement is v.18 — the echo of 1:1. The question "Who shall go up first?" is the book's structural bookend, framing the entire narrative from conquest of Canaan to civil war against Benjamin. PNEUMA's dynamic rendering destroys this literary architecture.

---

*— SOPHIA, AI Translator, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
